claim: Saccharomyces cerevisiae typically produces ~25 daughter cells before dying
source: The unicellular eukaryote Saccharomyces cerevisiae (budding yeast), which typically produces ~25 daughter cells before dying (Mortimer and Johnston, 1959), has enabled several insights into the cellular aging process via a combination of cell biological, genetic, and genomic approaches (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012; McCormick et al., 2015; Janssens et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2014; Defossez et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Mortimer and Johnston, 1959

claim: The rDNA locus contains ~100–200 tandemly repeated copies in the genome
source: For example, instability at the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) locus, which contains ~100–200 tandemly repeated copies in the genome, can result in the formation of rDNA extra-chromosomal circles (ERCs), and is is a major determinant of yeast replicative lifespan (RLS) (Defossez et al., 1999; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997; Kobayashi et al., 1998; Stumpferl et al., 2012; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on rDNA and ERCs

claim: rDNA instability can result in the formation of rDNA extra-chromosomal circles (ERCs)
source: For example, instability at the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) locus, which contains ~100–200 tandemly repeated copies in the genome, can result in the formation of rDNA extra-chromosomal circles (ERCs), and is is a major determinant of yeast replicative lifespan (RLS) (Defossez et al., 1999; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997; Kobayashi et al., 1998; Stumpferl et al., 2012; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations on rDNA instability and ERC formation

claim: rDNA instability is a major determinant of yeast replicative lifespan (RLS)
source: For example, instability at the ribosomal DNA (rDNA) locus, which contains ~100–200 tandemly repeated copies in the genome, can result in the formation of rDNA extra-chromosomal circles (ERCs), and is is a major determinant of yeast replicative lifespan (RLS) (Defossez et al., 1999; Sinclair and Guarente, 1997; Kobayashi et al., 1998; Stumpferl et al., 2012; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations on rDNA and RLS

claim: A single-nucleotide polymorphism that reduces the rate of origin firing at the rDNA locus increases rDNA stability and thereby increases RLS
source: A single-nucleotide polymorphism that reduces the rate of origin firing at the rDNA locus increases rDNA stability, and thereby increases RLS (Kwan et al., 2013; Foss et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kwan et al., 2013 and Foss et al., 2017

claim: A decrease in vacuolar acidity early in a mother cell's life promotes mitochondrial dysfunction and limits her lifespan
source: In a seemingly unrelated pathway, a decrease in vacuolar acidity early in a mother cell's life promotes mitochondrial dysfunction and limits her lifespan (Hughes and Gottschling, 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Hughes and Gottschling, 2012

claim: Caloric restriction-mediated life extension acts through the homeostatic regulator GCN4
source: Likewise, caloric restriction-mediated life extension, acting through the homeostatic regulator GCN4, is a well-studied yeast RLS intervention that is broadly phenocopied by perturbations that inhibit translation (Steffen et al., 2008; Mittal et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Steffen et al., 2008 and Mittal et al., 2017

claim: Caloric restriction-mediated life extension is broadly phenocopied by perturbations that inhibit translation
source: Likewise, caloric restriction-mediated life extension, acting through the homeostatic regulator GCN4, is a well-studied yeast RLS intervention that is broadly phenocopied by perturbations that inhibit translation (Steffen et al., 2008; Mittal et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to Steffen et al., 2008 and Mittal et al., 2017

claim: RLSs of >4500 gene deletions were recently measured using microdissection
source: In a step towards a systems-level understanding of the genetic determinants of cellular aging, RLSs of >4500 gene deletions were recently measured using microdissection to physically separate daughter cells from mother cells and manually counting the number of divisions before mother cell death (McCormick et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to McCormick et al., 2015

claim: Pre-growth in liquid culture after biotin labeling improved the uniformity of the number of beads per cell
source: Pre-growth in liquid culture after the biotin labeling improved the uniformity of the number of beads per cell, as compared to cells that were conjugated to beads immediately following biotin labeling.
evidence: Based on experimental observation in the study

claim: Purified mothers aged at the expected ~2 hr division rate in YNB glucose minimal media
source: We verified that purified mothers had aged at the expected ~2 hr division rate in YNB glucose minimal media by counting the number of replication bud scars for both haploid and diploid strains (38 hr: haploid = 15.5, diploid = 17.6; expected ~19) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Verified by bud scar counting data shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: At 38 hours, haploid cells had 15.5 bud scars and diploid cells had 17.6 bud scars (expected ~19)
source: We verified that purified mothers had aged at the expected ~2 hr division rate in YNB glucose minimal media by counting the number of replication bud scars for both haploid and diploid strains (38 hr: haploid = 15.5, diploid = 17.6; expected ~19) (Figure 1B and C).
evidence: Measured data from bud scar counting shown in Figure 1B and C

claim: Viability for aged sir2∆ mothers was ~2-fold lower than that of aged WT mothers
source: As expected, viability for aged sir2∆ mothers was ~2-fold lower than that of aged WT mothers (Figure 1D).
evidence: Measured viability data shown in Figure 1D

claim: Deletion of SIR2 shortens lifespan by promoting hyper-recombination at the rDNA locus
source: The deletion of the SIR2 NAD-dependent histone deacetylase shortens lifespan by promoting hyper-recombination at the rDNA locus (Kaeberlein et al., 1999; Gottlieb and Esposito, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kaeberlein et al., 1999 and Gottlieb and Esposito, 1989

claim: Some of the most upregulated transcripts with age were those arising from the rDNA locus, specifically from the Sir2p-silenced non-transcribed regions (NTS1 and NTS2)
source: Strikingly, some of the most upregulated transcripts were those arising from the rDNA locus, specifically from the Sir2p-silenced non-transcribed regions (NTS1 and NTS2).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis from the study

claim: Transcription at the non-transcribed sequence (NTS) locus is an aberrant Pol II event that is almost undetectable in log phase culture
source: Transcription at the non-transcribed sequence (NTS) locus is an aberrant Pol II event (almost undetectable in log phase culture) that has been previously shown to increase with age and ERC accumulation (Kobayashi and Ganley, 2005; Pal et al., 2018; Saka et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kobayashi and Ganley, 2005; Pal et al., 2018; Saka et al., 2013

claim: NTS transcription has been previously shown to increase with age and ERC accumulation
source: Transcription at the non-transcribed sequence (NTS) locus is an aberrant Pol II event (almost undetectable in log phase culture) that has been previously shown to increase with age and ERC accumulation (Kobayashi and Ganley, 2005; Pal et al., 2018; Saka et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kobayashi and Ganley, 2005; Pal et al., 2018; Saka et al., 2013

claim: Genes upregulated with age were enriched for terms related to metabolism, oxidoreductase activity, stress, and mitochondrial proteins
source: We found numerous significantly enriched terms related to metabolism, oxidoreductase activity, stress, and mitochondrial proteins amongst the genes whose expression increases with age (Source Data 1).
evidence: Based on DAVID GO-term enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data

claim: Genes downregulated with age were enriched for ribosome biogenesis, rRNA processing and translation
source: Genes downregulated with age were enriched for multiple terms, including ribosome biogenesis, rRNA processing and translation as well as a host of other terms related to general cellular anabolic function (tRNA synthesis, amino acid biosynthesis, mRNA transport, exosome activity) (Source Data 1).
evidence: Based on DAVID GO-term enrichment analysis of RNA-seq data

claim: The aging transcriptome shares a high degree of similarity to that of induction of the environmental stress response (ESR)
source: In general, these results are consistent with previous reports that the aging transcriptome shares a high degree of similarity to that of induction of the environmental stress response (ESR) (Janssens et al., 2015; Hu et al., 2014; Lesur and Campbell, 2004; Yiu et al., 2008; Kamei et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple previous studies and consistent with current data

claim: The ESR is the simultaneous activation of a set of stress-responsive pathways coincident with the downregulation of ribosomal biogenesis and is inextricably tied to growth rate
source: The ESR is the simultaneous activation of a set of stress-responsive pathways coincident with the downregulation of ribosomal biogenesis and it is inextricably tied to growth rate (i.e. if a yeast culture is growing slowly, the ESR is upregulated) (Brauer et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brauer et al., 2008

claim: A shift away from glycolysis toward gluconeogenesis was observed with age
source: Likewise, we also observed a shift away from glycolysis toward gluconeogenesis, similar to previous reports (Lin et al., 2001; Koc et al., 2004).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis and supported by citations to Lin et al., 2001 and Koc et al., 2004

claim: Almost all ESR-induced genes were upregulated with age and almost all ESR-repressed genes were downregulated
source: We found that a feature of the aging transcriptome is the activation of the ESR (i.e., almost all ESR-induced genes were upregulated with age and almost all ESR-repressed genes were downregulated [Figure 2]).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: TY transposon genes were highly enriched in ESR-independent age-induced gene clusters
source: Strikingly, this group of genes was highly enriched for TY transposon genes (Figure 2, Source Data 1).
evidence: Based on analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 2

claim: Age-dependent increases in transposon expression have been previously reported
source: Although age-dependent increases in transposon expression have been previously reported (Patterson et al., 2015), here we show that it is one of the earliest and strongest age-related changes (Figure 2, Source Data 1).
evidence: Supported by citation to Patterson et al., 2015 and current data shown in Figure 2

claim: Transposon upregulation is one of the earliest and strongest age-related changes
source: Although age-dependent increases in transposon expression have been previously reported (Patterson et al., 2015), here we show that it is one of the earliest and strongest age-related changes (Figure 2, Source Data 1).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: ADR1 was among early-age transcriptional responders and was previously reported to be an early-age transcriptional responder
source: The carbon source-responsive zinc-finger transcription factor, ADR1, was among these genes and was previously reported to be an early-age transcriptional responder (Kamei et al., 2014).
evidence: Based on current RNA-seq data and supported by citation to Kamei et al., 2014

claim: ADR1 has been previously found to be involved in regulating gluconeogenesis during the diauxic shift
source: ADR1 has also previously found to be involved in regulating gluconeogenesis during the diauxic shift, raising the possibility that ADR1 has a role in regulating the age induced transcriptional shift towards gluconeogenesis (Wierman et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wierman et al., 2017

claim: There is a negative correlation between transcript abundance during early age and age-related induction
source: In general, we observed a negative correlation between transcript abundance during early age and age-related induction (i.e. low abundance transcripts tend to undergo the largest fold increases; Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B

claim: Non-coding transcripts typically fell into the age-induced clusters
source: Interestingly, we also found that non-coding transcripts (Figure 2, right panel) typically fell into the age-induced clusters, similar to previous results (Sen et al., 2015).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 2 and supported by citation to Sen et al., 2015

claim: A recent study from Hu et al. suggested that all transcripts increase with age as a result of pervasive global transcription stemming from nucleosome loss
source: A recent study from Hu et al. suggested that all transcripts increase with age as a result of pervasive global transcription stemming from nucleosome loss (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) (Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: Citing Hu et al., 2014

claim: Universal up-regulation of gene expression is not a general feature of aging cells
source: Contrary to a previously published aging transcriptomic dataset (Hu et al., 2014), our data indicate that universal up-regulation of gene expression is not a general feature of aging cells.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis from the current study, contradicting Hu et al., 2014

claim: The discrepancy with Hu et al. may partially be due to batch effects in the previously published data
source: We suggest that this discrepancy may partially be due to batch effects in the previously published data (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on re-analysis of Hu et al. data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3

claim: Deletion of FOB1 can modulate yeast RLS by increasing rDNA stability and reducing ERC formation
source: Deletion of FOB1 can modulate yeast RLS by increasing rDNA stability and reducing ERC formation (Defossez et al., 1999; Takeuchi et al., 2003), whereas deleting UBR2 may confer longevity through constitutive upregulation of proteasome activity (Kruegel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Defossez et al., 1999 and Takeuchi et al., 2003

claim: Deleting UBR2 may confer longevity through constitutive upregulation of proteasome activity
source: Deletion of FOB1 can modulate yeast RLS by increasing rDNA stability and reducing ERC formation (Defossez et al., 1999; Takeuchi et al., 2003), whereas deleting UBR2 may confer longevity through constitutive upregulation of proteasome activity (Kruegel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Kruegel et al., 2011

claim: An apparent increase in expression of proteasome-related genes was observed in the sir2∆ strain
source: Surprisingly, we also observed an apparent increase in expression of proteasome-related genes in the sir2∆ strain (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B

claim: A significantly lower median bud scar age was observed at both aged time points for the sir2∆ strain compared to wild type
source: Importantly, we observed a significantly lower median bud scar age at both aged time points for the sir2∆ strain compared to wild type and slightly higher ages for ubr2∆ and fob1∆ compared to wild type in both the total population of collected cells and in the viable fraction (Figure 3—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Based on bud scar counting data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3

claim: Cell division slows in the approach to replicative senescence
source: That cell division slows in the approach to replicative senescence is a well-documented observation (Fehrmann et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Fehrmann et al., 2013

claim: The older bud scar age in fob1∆ and ubr2∆ is not a function of a faster growth rate per se, but rather a result of there being a higher percentage of actively dividing cells
source: Therefore, we reasoned that the older bud scar age in fob1∆ and ubr2∆ is not a function of a faster growth rate per se, but rather a result of there being a higher percentage of actively dividing cells in fob1∆ and ubr2∆ backgrounds.
evidence: Based on inference from bud scar data and known biology of cell division slowing

claim: The aging transcriptomes were similar across strains
source: Although the aging transcriptomes were similar, it was the paucity of significant differences that emphasizes how analogous the transcriptional aging profile appears across strains (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: For sir2∆, the significant differences were in most cases a matter of magnitude per replication event (bud scar)
source: Even for sir2∆, the strain that exhibited the strongest strain-specific response to aging, the significant differences were in most cases a matter of magnitude per replication event (bud scar); the same genes changed, only more so, reflective either of a higher aging rate or a larger percentage of cells close to replicative senescence (Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4

claim: An age-dependent expression decrease in five out of six components of the signal recognition particle (SRP) was observed
source: Notably, we observed an age-dependent expression decrease in five out of six components of the signal recognition particle (SRP).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis

claim: There is a strong correlation (r = −0.67) between rate of change with age and rate of change with growth rate for genes that increase with age and canonical ESR induced genes
source: We compared the rate of change with age (Figure 3B, y-axis) to the rate of change with growth rate (Figure 3B, x-axis) and found a strong correlation for genes that increase with age and canonical ESR induced genes (r = −0.67).
evidence: Based on comparison of aging slopes with growth rate slopes shown in Figure 3B

claim: The correlation for all genes between aging slope and growth rate slope is strong (r = −0.48)
source: In general, the correlation for all genes (r = −0.48) was strong and underscores the close relationship between RLS, stress, and growth rate.
evidence: Based on comparison of aging slopes with growth rate slopes

claim: Genes with an age-related increase in expression that are not strongly dependent on the GRS are greatly enriched for genes coding for transmembrane helices and those classified as secreted and/or containing sequence for a signal recognition peptide (SRP binding site)
source: We found that genes with an age-related increase in expression that are not strongly dependent on the GRS are greatly enriched for genes coding for transmembrane helices and more specifically for those that are classified as secreted and/or of containing sequence for a signal recognition peptide (SRP binding site) (Source Data 2).
evidence: Based on GO term analysis of RNA-seq data

claim: SRP clients are, as a class of genes, significantly upregulated with age in a GRS-independent manner (p<10−51)
source: We found that these SRP clients are, as a class of genes, significantly upregulated with age in a GRS-independent manner (p<10−51, hypergeometric, Figure 3C).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Expression of SRP subunits and SRP clients was strongly negatively correlated (r ~ −0.5) across the yeast deleteome dataset
source: Expression of SRP subunits and SRP clients was strongly negatively correlated (r ~ −0.5), suggesting the existence of a negative feedback loop between SRP and its clients.
evidence: Based on analysis of data from Kemmeren et al., 2014 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 5

claim: SCR1 is increasing roughly two-fold from ~5% to~10% of the transcriptome with age
source: The aggregate trend across all of the genotypes we assayed indicates that SCR1 is increasing roughly two-fold from ~5% to~10% of the transcriptome with age (Figure 3D).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3D

claim: Genes involved in ER-associated protein degradation, specifically the members of the Cdc48p-Npl4p-Ufd1p segregase complex, were upregulated with age
source: Genes involved in ER-associated protein degradation, specifically the members of the Cdc48p-Npl4p-Ufd1p segregase complex, were upregulated with age (Figure 3C, orange dots) and are not canonical ESR genes.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data shown in Figure 3C

claim: Previous work has suggested a loss of silencing at subtelomeric regions potentially as a result of redistribution of SIR proteins from telomeres to the nucleolus
source: In addition, previous work has suggested a loss of silencing at subtelomeric regions, potentially as a result of redistribution of SIR proteins from telomeres to the nucleolus, follows from an increasing rDNA copy number and age-dependent nucleolar dysfunction that is not dependent on telomere length (Kennedy et al., 1997; Salvi et al., 2013; Kim et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Kennedy et al., 1997; Salvi et al., 2013; Kim et al., 1996

claim: Genes located in subtelomeric regions are more likely to increase in expression with age
source: We found that genes located in subtelomeric regions are more likely to increase in expression with age (Figure 3—figure supplement 7A).
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7A

claim: Subtelomeric genes as a group have a negative GRS and thus increase in expression as a function of slower growth rate
source: We plotted the GRS versus distance from the telomeres and found that indeed, subtelomeric genes as a group have a negative GRS and thus increase in expression as a function of slower growth rate (Figure 3—figure supplement 7B).
evidence: Based on analysis of GRS data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 7B

claim: It was recently suggested that old cells have a globally lower nucleosomal occupancy that could result in permissive transcription and genomic instability
source: It was recently suggested that old cells have a globally lower nucleosomal occupancy that could result in permissive transcription and genomic instability (Hu et al., 2014).
evidence: Citing Hu et al., 2014

claim: Nucleosomes protect DNA from transposition by Tn5, resulting in depletion of Tn5 insertions in a region of about 140 bases around the centers of nucleosomes
source: Nucleosomes protect DNA from transposition by Tn5, resulting in depletion of Tn5 insertions in a region of about 140 bases around the centers of nucleosomes (Figure 4A) (Brogaard et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brogaard et al., 2012 and shown in Figure 4A

claim: ATAC-seq samples from the old cells contained a higher level of background insertions
source: We noticed, however, that ATAC-seq samples from the old cells contained a higher level of background insertions.
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data analysis

claim: Mid-gene bodies that are normally inaccessible to ATAC-seq became uniformly more accessible in old cells
source: For instance, mid-gene bodies that are normally inaccessible to ATAC-seq became uniformly more accessible (Figure 4B).
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4B

claim: The accessibility of canonically open nucleosome-free regions (NFRs) decreased with age
source: Consistent with this hypothesis, the accessibility of canonically open nucleosome-free regions (NFRs) decreased with age (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A

claim: DNA from dead cells has been a prominent confounder in microbiological studies as extracellular DNA can remain stable for days
source: DNA from the dead cells loses its chromatin structure, yielding an ATAC-seq signal that is virtually uniform (Figure 4—figure supplement 2). Because the number of dead cells recovered (Figure 1D) increases with age, we hypothesized that the non-specific background in the ATAC-seq signal could rise because of the contamination by dead cells in old cultures. Since dead cells lose their membrane integrity, their DNA can be made inert to the ATAC-seq amplification by pre-treatment with intercalating agent propidium monoazide (PMA). PMA selectively enters dead cells and upon photo-activation binds covalently to DNA, strongly inhibiting its amplification in subsequent PCR reactions.
evidence: Supported by citation to Nielsen et al., 2007

claim: PMA can effectively remove the 'dead cell' signature from mixed samples
source: Testing the efficacy of PMA treatment in yeast on heat-killed cells revealed that PMA can effectively remove the 'dead cell' signature from mixed samples (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Based on experimental data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claim: Addition of PMA decreased the accessibility of nucleosomal DNA in the old sample to the level observed in the young sample
source: Strikingly, addition of PMA decreased the accessibility of nucleosomal DNA in the old sample to the level observed in the young sample (Figure 4A), and this PMA-dependent decrease in accessibility was specific to the old cells (>30 hr) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B

claim: Without PMA treatment, average nucleosomal occupancy declined with age
source: Indeed, without PMA treatment, average nucleosomal occupancy declined with age. This decline in occupancy, however, nearly disappeared when the samples were treated with PMA (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on NucleoATAC analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: The decline in nucleosomal occupancy with age nearly disappeared when the samples were treated with PMA
source: Indeed, without PMA treatment, average nucleosomal occupancy declined with age. This decline in occupancy, however, nearly disappeared when the samples were treated with PMA (Figure 4C).
evidence: Based on NucleoATAC analysis shown in Figure 4C

claim: The nucleosomal occupancy remains constant, on average, with age when comparing PMA-treated daughter cells to mother cells
source: These findings were further supported by comparing occupancy of the PMA-treated daughter cell fraction (flow-through) to that of the middle aged and old mother cell fractions in three biological replicates (Figure 4D). Also here, we observed that the nucleosomal occupancy remains constant, on average, with age (Figure 4D).
evidence: Based on NucleoATAC analysis shown in Figure 4D

claim: The global chromatin structure does not deteriorate significantly with age
source: We conclude that the global chromatin structure does not deteriorate significantly with age and previous observations to the contrary may be explained by an increase in the proportion of the dead cells in the aging population.
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data analysis with PMA treatment

claim: Previous observations of global chromatin deterioration with age may be explained by an increase in the proportion of dead cells in the aging population
source: We conclude that the global chromatin structure does not deteriorate significantly with age and previous observations to the contrary may be explained by an increase in the proportion of the dead cells in the aging population.
evidence: Based on inference from ATAC-seq data with and without PMA treatment

claim: Local changes in chromatin structure with age were observed
source: Although global chromatin structure did not change significantly between the young and the old cells, local changes in chromatin structure with age were observed (Figure 4—figure supplement 4A), suggesting that the activities of multiple transcription factors and chromatin remodelers change with age.
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4A

claim: At a q-value of 10−3, approximately 12% of genomic bins were significantly opening or closing in all strains
source: We set the significance cutoff at a q-value of 10−3. At this q-value approximately 12% of bins were significantly opening or closing in all strains (Figure 5A, Figure 4—figure supplement 4B, Source Data 3).
evidence: Based on statistical analysis of ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 4—figure supplement 4B

claim: Bins located in gene bodies tended to preferentially open with age
source: Bins located in gene bodies tended to preferentially open, while promoters tended to preferentially close. Origins of replications (ARS) strongly tended to lose accessibility (Figure 5A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4C,D

claim: Promoters tended to preferentially close with age
source: Bins located in gene bodies tended to preferentially open, while promoters tended to preferentially close. Origins of replications (ARS) strongly tended to lose accessibility (Figure 5A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4C,D

claim: Origins of replications (ARS) strongly tended to lose accessibility with age
source: Bins located in gene bodies tended to preferentially open, while promoters tended to preferentially close. Origins of replications (ARS) strongly tended to lose accessibility (Figure 5A,B, Figure 4—figure supplement 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 4D).
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 5A,B and Figure 4—figure supplement 4C,D

claim: A similar closing of ARS elements occurs during the transition from the reductive to oxidative phase of the metabolic cycle
source: Comparing with other ATAC-seq datasets in yeast, we found that a similar closing of ARS elements occurs during the transition from the reductive to oxidative phase of the metabolic cycle (Gowans et al., 2018) (Figure 4—figure supplement 4E).
evidence: Based on comparison with data from Gowans et al., 2018 shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4E

claim: DNA replication is inhibited in aging mothers
source: Since the reductive phase is characterized by a global decrease in DNA replication, our results suggests that DNA replication is inhibited in aging mothers.
evidence: Based on inference from ATAC-seq data showing ARS closure and comparison with metabolic cycle data

claim: Bins that increase in accessibility were highly enriched for binding of multiple transcription factors, including cell cycle regulators (Ndd1, Swi4/6, Fkh1/2 and Sbp1), and regulators of amino acid biogenesis, particularly Arg81, Leu3 and Gcn4
source: No strong enrichment was found in bins that decrease in accessibility, but bins that increase in accessibility were highly enriched for binding of multiple transcription factors, including cell cycle regulators (Ndd1, Swi4/6, Fkh1/2 and Sbp1), and regulators of amino acid biogenesis, particularly Arg81, Leu3 and Gcn4 (Figure 5B, Source Data 4).
evidence: Based on enrichment analysis of ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 5B

claim: All enzymes in leucine biosynthesis superpathway and all enzymes in arginine biosynthesis pathway besides Arg2 and Arg7 gained accessibility with age
source: Notably, all enzymes in leucine biosynthesis superpathway and all enzymes in arginine biosynthesis pathway besides Arg2 and Arg7 gained accessibility with age.
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data analysis

claim: The aging slopes estimated in WT, ubr2∆ and fob1∆ were highly correlated with a slope of one
source: The aging slopes estimated in WT, ubr2∆ and fob1∆ were highly correlated with a slope of one. Sir2∆ cells, however, behaved quite differently, with all slopes significantly higher than in the wild type, which we interpret as faster rate of aging in this background.
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4F

claim: Sir2∆ cells had all slopes significantly higher than in the wild type, which is interpreted as faster rate of aging in this background
source: The aging slopes estimated in WT, ubr2∆ and fob1∆ were highly correlated with a slope of one. Sir2∆ cells, however, behaved quite differently, with all slopes significantly higher than in the wild type, which we interpret as faster rate of aging in this background.
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data analysis and interpretation

claim: Although the slopes of changes were higher in sir2∆ overall, the slopes were highly correlated, suggesting that the overall pattern of age-dependent change in accessibility remains the same in this mutant strain
source: Notably, however, although the slopes of changes were higher in sir2∆ overall, the slopes were highly correlated, suggesting that the overall pattern of age-dependent change in accessibility remains the same in this mutant strain (Figure 4—figure supplement 4F).
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4F

claim: With age, WT strains present with a ~ 2 fold increase in insertional density over the entire rDNA locus
source: We found that with age, WT strains present with a ~ 2 fold increase in insertional density over the entire rDNA locus (Figure 6, first panel).
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6

claim: rDNA copy number increased with age in WT cells
source: To determine whether the observed increase in ATAC-seq coverage at the rDNA locus (Figure 6A) was driven by increased accessibility (1) versus copy number expansion (2 and 3), we quantified relative rDNA copy number using qPCR with DNA from aged samples, and found that rDNA copy number increased with age (Figure 6B).
evidence: Based on qPCR data shown in Figure 6B

claim: In comparison to insertional density, relative copy number increases to a larger extent with age, suggesting that the age-dependent increase in insertional density at the rDNA locus is largely being driven by copy number expansion
source: In fact, in comparison to insertional density, relative copy number increases to a larger extent with age, suggesting that the age-dependent increase in insertional density at the rDNA locus is largely being driven by copy number expansion.
evidence: Based on comparison of ATAC-seq and qPCR data

claim: The increased ATAC-seq signal at the rDNA locus returned to normal levels in daughters born to old mothers, demonstrating an asymmetric division of signal
source: We observed that the increased ATAC-seq signal at the rDNA locus returned to normal levels in daughters born to old mothers, demonstrating an asymmetric division of signal.
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data from daughter cells

claim: Increasing ATAC-seq insertion density at the rDNA locus is reflective of greater numbers of asymmetrically retained ERC rDNA repeats with age
source: Together, these data argue for (3): increasing ATAC-seq insertion density at the rDNA locus is reflective of greater numbers of asymmetrically retained ERC rDNA repeats with age.
evidence: Based on inference from ATAC-seq and qPCR data showing asymmetric retention

claim: Sir2∆ cells had slightly more (~20%) relative rDNA copy number than WT at young ages
source: Sir2∆ cells had slightly more (~20%) relative rDNA copy number than WT at young ages (Figure 6A,B) but much higher ATAC-seq coverage (twofold).
evidence: Based on qPCR and ATAC-seq data shown in Figure 6A,B

claim: In sir2∆, relative rDNA copy number increased by ~10 fold and ATAC-seq signal only increased by twofold at older ages
source: However, in looking at age-related increases at this locus in sir2∆, relative rDNA copy number increased by ~10 fold and ATAC-seq signal only increased by twofold at older ages; one interpretation of these data is that an initial open chromatin state may promote instability/higher copy number with age.
evidence: Based on qPCR and ATAC-seq data

claim: An initial open chromatin state may promote instability/higher copy number with age
source: However, in looking at age-related increases at this locus in sir2∆, relative rDNA copy number increased by ~10 fold and ATAC-seq signal only increased by twofold at older ages; one interpretation of these data is that an initial open chromatin state may promote instability/higher copy number with age.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of ATAC-seq and qPCR data

claim: fob1∆ cells begin with ~15% higher relative rDNA copy number compared to WT during log phase
source: Surprisingly, like the sir2∆ strain, fob1∆ cells begin with ~15% higher relative rDNA copy number compared to WT during log phase, and have actually ~20% higher accessibility as measured by rDNA ATAC-seq than WT, consistent with the role of Fob1p in Sir2p recruitment to the rDNA (Huang and Moazed, 2003).
evidence: Based on qPCR and ATAC-seq data, consistent with citation to Huang and Moazed, 2003

claim: fob1∆ cells have ~20% higher accessibility as measured by rDNA ATAC-seq than WT, consistent with the role of Fob1p in Sir2p recruitment to the rDNA
source: Surprisingly, like the sir2∆ strain, fob1∆ cells begin with ~15% higher relative rDNA copy number compared to WT during log phase, and have actually ~20% higher accessibility as measured by rDNA ATAC-seq than WT, consistent with the role of Fob1p in Sir2p recruitment to the rDNA (Huang and Moazed, 2003).
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq data and supported by citation to Huang and Moazed, 2003

claim: fob1∆ cells experience a much more modest increase in both ATAC-seq signal (1.4 fold vs 2.5 fold) and relative copy number (1.6-fold vs 6-fold) with age compared to WT
source: We find that fob1∆ cells experience a much more modest increase in both ATAC-seq signal (1.4 fold vs 2.5 fold) and relative copy number (1.6-fold vs 6-fold) with age.
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq and qPCR data

claim: fob1∆ is only partially defective in ERC formation
source: Importantly, we note that if the source of our increased ATAC-seq rDNA coverage and estimated relative rDNA copy number are in fact from ERC build up, fob1∆ is only partially defective in ERC formation, consistent with previous work (Lindstrom et al., 2011).
evidence: Based on inference from ATAC-seq and qPCR data, consistent with citation to Lindstrom et al., 2011

claim: In young cells, rDNA ATAC-seq signal and relative copy number for ubr2∆ was equivalent to WT
source: In young cells, rDNA ATAC-seq signal and relative copy number for ubr2∆ was equivalent to WT.
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq and qPCR data

claim: With age, ubr2∆ cells displayed an attenuated rDNA phenotype compared to WT in both ATAC-seq (1.7 vs 2.5) and relative copy number (2.3 vs 6)
source: With age, however, the ubr2∆ cells displayed an attenuated rDNA phenotype compared to WT in both ATAC-seq (1.7 vs 2.5) and relative copy number (2.3 vs 6).
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq and qPCR data

claim: It has previously been shown that the nucleoli of aged yeast cells grow large and fragment
source: In yeast cells, rDNA is localized, transcribed, processed and assembled into ribosomes within the nucleolar subcompartment of the nucleus (Taddei and Gasser, 2012). It has previously been shown that the nucleoli of aged yeast cells grow large and fragment (Sinclair et al., 1997).
evidence: Supported by citations to Taddei and Gasser, 2012 and Sinclair et al., 1997

claim: Old cells from all genotypes showed nucleolar enlargement compared to young cells
source: Compared to young cells, old cells from all genotypes showed nucleolar enlargement (Figure 7).
evidence: Based on microscopy data shown in Figure 7

claim: The observed increases in nucleolar size were clearly more pronounced in WT and sir2∆ than in ubr2∆ and fob1∆
source: However, the observed increases were clearly more pronounced in WT and sir2∆ than in ubr2∆ and fob1∆, similar to what was seen in the qPCR and ATAC-seq assays.
evidence: Based on microscopy data shown in Figure 7

claim: A dominant feature of the transcriptional response to aging is the activation of the ESR, characterized by the induction of stress response factors and a repression of ribosome biogenesis programs
source: We found in our analysis of the transcriptional response to aging that a dominant feature is the activation of the ESR, characterized by the induction of stress response factors and a repression of ribosome biogenesis programs.
evidence: Based on RNA-seq data analysis

claim: Deleting both MSN2 and MSN4 does not reduce RLS on rich medium
source: A previous study provided evidence that deleting both of the primary ESR-related transcription factors, MSN2 and MSN4, does not reduce RLS on rich medium (where all of the amino acids are provided); it was also found that these same transcription factors are required for lifespan extension under conditions of lowered glucose (Medvedik et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Medvedik et al., 2007

claim: MSN2 and MSN4 are required for lifespan extension under conditions of lowered glucose
source: A previous study provided evidence that deleting both of the primary ESR-related transcription factors, MSN2 and MSN4, does not reduce RLS on rich medium (where all of the amino acids are provided); it was also found that these same transcription factors are required for lifespan extension under conditions of lowered glucose (Medvedik et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Medvedik et al., 2007

claim: The concordance between aging and ESR follows from a cascade of cellular decline that results in age-associated slowing of growth
source: Currently, we favor a model in which the concordance we observe follows from a cascade of cellular decline that results in age-associated slowing of growth, which is consistent with reports of age-dependent reductions in single-cell budding rates measured in microfluidics devices (Jo et al., 2015).
evidence: Speculative model supported by citation to Jo et al., 2015

claim: Sub-telomeric regions are fast-evolving and the genes therein are enriched for being related to stress, cell surface properties, and carbohydrate metabolism
source: It was previously shown that sub-telomeric regions are fast-evolving and the genes therein are enriched for being related to stress, cell surface properties, and carbohydrate metabolism, all of which are enriched functional annotations in our pan-aging gene expression signature (Brown et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Brown et al., 2010

claim: The high evolvability of subtelomeric regions permits rapid adaptation to novel stresses
source: Those authors speculated that the high evolvability of subtelomeric regions permits rapid adaptation to novel stresses (Brown et al., 2010).
evidence: Citing speculation from Brown et al., 2010

claim: Histone mRNAs and proteins have been reported to decline with replicative age in yeast
source: Histone mRNAs and proteins have been reported to decline with replicative age in yeast (Hu et al., 2014; Pal et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hu et al., 2014 and Pal et al., 2018

claim: A model exists wherein reductions in histone protein lower the number of functional nucleosomes, resulting in erosion of appropriate transcriptional control which manifests as a universal upregulation of all transcripts
source: This observation, in tandem with a systematic measurement of nucleosome occupancy, have accreted into a model wherein the reductions in histone protein lower the number of functional nucleosomes. The loss of nucleosomes is then purported to result in the erosion of appropriate transcriptional control which manifests as a universal upregulation of all transcripts.
evidence: Describing a model from the literature

claim: The modified ATAC-seq method will become a generally useful approach for exploring genomic changes in mixed-viability samples
source: It is our expectation that our modified ATAC-seq method will become a generally useful approach for exploring genomic changes in mixed-viability samples.
evidence: Speculative statement about future utility

claim: In an aging yeast population, a smaller fraction of cells are in S-phase and thus depleted for active replication, resulting in the observed decline in accessibility at origins of replication
source: Through comparison to other ATAC-seq datasets, we hypothesize that in an aging yeast population, a smaller fraction of cells are in S-phase and thus depleted for active replication, resulting in the observed decline in accessibility at origins of replication.
evidence: Hypothesis based on ATAC-seq data and comparison with other datasets

claim: ERC formation may be a common cause of replicative senescence in S. cerevisiae across numerous strain backgrounds and environments
source: Changes in the rDNA stability with age manifest as ERC formation, which may be a common cause of replicative senescence in S. cerevisiae across numerous strain backgrounds and environments.
evidence: Speculative statement based on data and literature

claim: The aged ubr2∆ rDNA profile phenocopies that of fob1∆
source: We also found that the aged ubr2∆ rDNA profile phenocopies that of fob1∆, an unexpected result given that UBR2 is believed to confer longevity through proteasome activation independently of FOB1 and SIR2.
evidence: Based on ATAC-seq and qPCR data

claim: These results provide provocative evidence that UBR2 is involved in ERC formation/rDNA stability
source: Overall, these results are consistent with the known roles of SIR2 and FOB1 and provide provocative evidence that UBR2 is involved in ERC formation/rDNA stability.
evidence: Based on inference from ATAC-seq and qPCR data

claim: Combining the MAD platform with single-cell analysis could be especially informative
source: In the future, our expectation is that combining the MAD platform with single-cell analysis could be especially informative.
evidence: Speculative statement about future applications

claim: Single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq could facilitate the identification of distinct aging trajectories where subtle causative changes can be distinguished from unsubtle stress responses
source: MAD provides the means to obtain aged cells, which can then be investigated with sequencing and optical methods; indeed, it is our expectation that single-cell RNA-seq and ATAC-seq could facilitate the identification of distinct aging trajectories where subtle causative changes can be distinguished from unsubtle stress responses (Bendall et al., 2014; Trapnell et al., 2014), making it easier to separate cause from effect.
evidence: Speculative statement about future applications, supported by citations to Bendall et al., 2014 and Trapnell et al., 2014

claim: Ring magnets enable an even distribution of magnetically labeled mother cells along the glass walls of the MAD
source: Ring magnets are an important component of the system because they enable an even distribution of magnetically labeled mother cells along the glass walls of the MAD (i.e. they help minimize clumping).
evidence: Based on experimental design and observation

claim: The optical density (OD600) of the culture media within the MAD was kept at less than 0.15 to ensure that pH and glucose remained constant in the vessels
source: The optical density (OD600) of the culture media within the MAD was kept at less than 0.15 to ensure that pH and glucose remained constant in the vessels (data not shown).
evidence: Based on experimental measurements (data not shown)

claim: Keeping the bead-to-cell ratio at <20:1 is important; increasing the number of beads per cell can greatly inhibit growth
source: It is worth noting that keeping the bead-to-cell ratio at <20:1 is important; increasing the number of beads per cell can greatly inhibit growth (Figure 1—figure supplement 6).
evidence: Based on experimental observation shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 6
